topic_title: Top 10 Best Dog Breeds for Cold Weather
intro: Every breed on this list handles cold well, so the real choice is about what living with the dog is like the rest of the year. Dense double coats that keep a dog warm in January shed heavily in spring, often by the handful. Many cold-climate breeds are large or giant, which affects car size, food costs and lifespan. Some were bred to bark at game or pull sleds for hours, and that drive does not switch off indoors. Also think about summer, because thick-coated dogs struggle in heat and need shade and cooler walk times.

picks.description: The Chow Chow has one of the thickest coats of any breed, which keeps it comfortable in cold weather, and its energy is low, so 20 to 30 minutes of walking a day is enough. It is placed last because of temperament. Chows are independent, aloof and protective, they are hard to train, and they are rated not good with children, cats or other dogs. They usually bond with one or two people and stay reserved with everyone else, so early socialization matters a great deal. The dense coat sheds heavily and needs brushing several times a week to prevent mats. Chows weigh about 45 to 70 pounds, have very low heat tolerance, and their deep-set eyes need regular checks.
picks.best_for: Experienced adult owners wanting a quiet, independent, low-energy dog
picks.quirky_fact: Chow Chows have blue-black tongues, a trait shared with the Shar-Pei.
picks.skip_if: You have children, cats or other dogs, or are a first-time owner

picks.description: The Finnish Spitz is a fox-colored hunting dog from Finland, about 20 to 33 pounds, with a medium double coat that copes well with northern winters. It is playful and friendly, and rated good with children, cats and other dogs. Coat care is moderate: weekly brushing, with more during seasonal shedding, and less hair overall than most breeds here. The defining trait is its voice. Finnish Spitz were bred to bark repeatedly to point birds for hunters, and they are rated high for barking, which makes them hard to keep in apartments or close neighborhoods. They are independent and only moderately easy to train, and they need about an hour of activity a day. The breed is rare outside Scandinavia.
picks.best_for: Rural cold-climate owners wanting a lighter, medium-sized spitz
picks.quirky_fact: Finland holds barking competitions for the Finnish Spitz, which is known as the barking bird dog.
picks.skip_if: You live near neighbors or want a quiet dog that trains easily

picks.description: The Keeshond is a Dutch barge dog with a long, thick coat and a plush ruff that make it comfortable in cold, damp weather. It is friendly, playful and easy to train, and rated good with children, cats and other dogs, so it suits family life well. At about 35 to 45 pounds it is easier to handle than the giant breeds here, and 30 to 45 minutes of exercise a day keeps it content. The main drawback is barking: Keeshonden are rated high and will announce anything that moves, so they need early training and are a poor fit for thin-walled housing. The coat sheds heavily and needs brushing a few times a week, and they want company rather than long hours alone.
picks.best_for: Families wanting a friendly, trainable, medium-sized cold-weather dog
picks.quirky_fact: Keeshonden were kept on Dutch river barges as watchdogs, which explains their alert voice.
picks.skip_if: You share walls with neighbors or can't teach a quiet cue

picks.description: The Finnish Lapphund herded reindeer above the Arctic Circle, and its long, thick coat is made for snow and wind. It is a manageable medium size of about 33 to 53 pounds, and it combines easy training with a calm, affectionate nature that is rated good with children, cats and other dogs. Expect to give 45 to 60 minutes of walks and play a day. Lappies are herders, so they may chase or nip at running children unless taught otherwise, and they bark at a medium level. The coat sheds heavily, especially during seasonal blows, and needs brushing at least weekly. They have low heat tolerance, and because the breed is rare, finding a puppy can take time.
picks.best_for: Owners wanting a cold-hardy dog in a manageable size
picks.quirky_fact: Finnish Lapphunds were bred to herd reindeer by circling and barking rather than nipping.
picks.skip_if: You live somewhere hot or need a puppy quickly

picks.description: The Norwegian Elkhound is a medium-sized Scandinavian hunting dog, around 48 to 55 pounds, with a thick gray double coat that sheds snow and holds warmth. It is friendly and loyal with its family and rated good with children, cats and other dogs, while staying alert and protective of the house. Elkhounds need about an hour of activity a day and enjoy long walks in the snow. They are independent, so training takes patience and short, varied sessions. The coat sheds heavily and needs brushing several times a week, more in spring and fall. They bark at a medium level, and they love food, so measure meals to prevent weight gain.
picks.best_for: Active owners wanting a sturdy, medium-sized winter hiking dog
picks.quirky_fact: Elkhounds were used to track moose and hold them at bay by barking until the hunter arrived.
picks.skip_if: You want a quick learner or dislike heavy seasonal shedding

picks.description: The Greater Swiss Mountain Dog was bred as an Alpine draft and farm dog, and its short, dense coat is better suited to cold than its smooth look suggests. It is the easiest coat on this list: grooming is low, a weekly brush is enough most of the year, and shedding is moderate rather than heavy. Swissies are friendly, loyal and calm, and rated good with children, cats and other dogs. Expect 30 to 60 minutes of exercise a day, plus a job such as carting or hiking if you can offer it. They bark at a medium level and can be protective of their home. Adults weigh about 85 to 140 pounds, puppies mature slowly, and the lifespan is around 8 to 11 years.
picks.best_for: Cold-climate owners wanting a big dog with an easy coat
picks.quirky_fact: Swissies were once called the poor man's horse because farmers used them to pull carts to market.
picks.skip_if: You want a long-lived dog or can't handle a strong puller

picks.description: The Leonberger is a German giant with a long, water-resistant double coat and a thick mane, comfortable in snow, wet cold and lake water. It is gentle, calm and rated good with children, cats and other dogs, and it seldom barks, which makes it a steady family dog for people who have the space. Energy is moderate: about an hour of walks, hiking or swimming a day keeps it content. Males can reach 110 to 170 pounds, so early leash training and socialization matter. The coat sheds heavily and needs brushing several times a week, with extra work in shedding season. Like most giant breeds it has a short lifespan of around 8 to 9 years, and vet and food costs are high.
picks.best_for: Families with room who want a calm, water-loving giant
picks.quirky_fact: The Leonberger was developed in the town of Leonberg, Germany, whose coat of arms features a lion.
picks.skip_if: You live in a small home or can't budget for giant-dog costs

picks.description: The Samoyed was bred by Siberian reindeer herders to herd, pull sleds and sleep beside people for warmth, and its dense white coat handles deep cold well. Among the snow breeds it is one of the easiest to live with: friendly, affectionate, easy to train and rated good with children, cats and other dogs. Energy is moderate, so 45 to 60 minutes of walks and play a day suits most adults, which weigh about 35 to 65 pounds. The big commitment is the coat. It sheds heavily, needs brushing several times a week to stop mats, and leaves white hair on everything during seasonal blows. Samoyeds bark at a medium level and dislike being alone for long, and they overheat easily in summer.
picks.best_for: Families in cold climates wanting a friendly, trainable snow dog
picks.quirky_fact: The upturned corners of a Samoyed's mouth help stop drool from freezing into icicles on its face.
picks.skip_if: You want a low-shedding dog or the dog will be alone all day

picks.description: The Alaskan Malamute is a freight sled dog, built to pull heavy loads over long distances in Arctic cold, and its thick double coat makes subzero walks comfortable. It is friendly with people and children and usually fine with other dogs, but its prey drive means it is not reliable with cats. Energy is high: plan on at least an hour of hard exercise a day, ideally pulling, hiking or skijoring. Malamutes are independent thinkers and only moderately easy to train, so they reward patient, consistent owners. Expect heavy shedding with two big coat blows a year, plenty of digging and talkative howling rather than barking. Adults weigh around 75 to 85 pounds and struggle in hot weather.
picks.best_for: Active owners who hike, ski or want a dog that pulls
picks.quirky_fact: Malamutes tend to talk with a woo-woo howl rather than bark at the door.
picks.skip_if: You have cats, a small yard, little time for exercise, or hot summers

picks.description: The Saint Bernard was bred in the Swiss Alps to work in deep snow, and its heavy frame and dense coat let it enjoy weather that sends most dogs back indoors. What puts it first is temperament: it is calm, gentle and rated good with children, cats and other dogs, and it rarely barks. Energy is low, so a 30 to 45 minute walk plus some time in the yard is usually enough. The trade-offs are size and upkeep. Adults commonly weigh 120 to 180 pounds, drool a lot, shed heavily and need brushing a few times a week. Training needs to start early, because a pulling adult is hard to hold on icy pavement. The lifespan of 8 to 10 years is short, and heat is a real risk in summer.
picks.best_for: Snowy homes with space wanting a calm, gentle giant
picks.quirky_fact: Saint Bernards were kept by monks at the Great St Bernard Pass to help find travelers lost in snow.
picks.skip_if: You have a small car or home, dislike drool, or live where summers are hot

faqs.question: What is the best dog breed for very cold climates?
faqs.answer: The Alaskan Malamute and Samoyed were bred to work in Arctic conditions and have dense double coats that insulate well below freezing. The Saint Bernard and Leonberger are calmer alternatives built for alpine winters. Even these breeds need shelter, dry bedding and fresh unfrozen water, and none should be left outside for long periods in extreme cold or wind.

faqs.question: Do cold weather dogs do badly in summer?
faqs.answer: Most do struggle in heat. The Saint Bernard, Malamute, Samoyed, Finnish Lapphund and Chow Chow are rated low for heat tolerance, so they need air conditioning, shade and walks in the early morning or late evening on hot days. Never shave a double coat to cool a dog down, since the coat also protects against sunburn and regrows unevenly.

faqs.question: How much do cold weather dogs shed?
faqs.answer: Nearly all of these breeds shed heavily, and double-coated dogs blow their undercoat once or twice a year, losing large clumps over a few weeks. Brushing several times a week with an undercoat rake and a slicker brush keeps the hair under control. The Greater Swiss Mountain Dog and Finnish Spitz shed less than the others on this list.

faqs.question: Which cold weather dogs are best with children?
faqs.answer: The Saint Bernard, Leonberger, Samoyed and Greater Swiss Mountain Dog are known for gentle, steady temperaments with children, though giant breeds can knock over toddlers by accident. The Chow Chow is not recommended for homes with kids because it tends to be aloof and protective. Always supervise young children with any dog, whatever the breed.

faqs.question: Do cold weather dogs need boots or coats in winter?
faqs.answer: Most of these breeds do not need a coat, because their double coat does the job. Paws are a different matter: road salt and de-icers can irritate pads, and snow can ball up between the toes of long-haired breeds. Rinse and dry paws after winter walks, trim the fur between pads, or use dog boots if your area salts heavily.

seo_title: Cold Weather Dog Breeds: 10 Snow-Ready Picks (2026)
answer: The Saint Bernard, Alaskan Malamute and Samoyed are the best cold weather dogs here: each was bred for snow and copes well with freezing temperatures. The deciding factor after coat is daily life, so match the dog's size, energy and shedding to your home, not just to your winters.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds rated high for cold tolerance, then ordered them by how well each fits a typical home: compatibility with children, cats and other dogs, barking level and trainability.
author: Elena Marsh
